newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Swedish deflation boosts hopes for rate cuts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Swedish deflation boosts hopes for rate cuts.

text.p: Sweden's inflation fell below zero for the first time in 37 years on Thursday and analysts said the deflationary moves would encourage the central bank, the Riksbank, to continue its policy of lowering interest rates.

Sweden's central statistics bureau, Statistics Sweden said the Consumer Price Index (CPI) was unchanged in October, giving a negative annualised inflation rate of minus 0.1 percent compared to a 2.7 percent rate a year ago.
"For the first time since 1959 the price changes over the past year are negative," Statistics Sweden said in statement.
Statistics Sweden said lower interest rates and lower value added tax on food were the main reasons for the fall.

"Food prices have fallen by 6.7 percent (over the year), which has reduced the overall price level by one percent," Statistics Sweden said. "Lower interest rate costs have contributed a further 1.1 percent to the fall."
Economists said the data was a little better than expected and should prompt continued interest rate cuts.
"It's hard to argue against a rate cut when Sweden is in deflation," HSBC Midland analyst Peter Lindqvist told Reuters.
But analysts cautioned that Sweden's unique CPI includes mortgage interest rates, so the headline inflation rate could not be taken at face value.
"This is why continuing falls in inflation don't necessarily translate into a more upbeat view on monetary policy," one London-based economist said.

Katharine Hoyland from JP Morgan said Sweden's CPI had benefited from lower mortgage interest rates and also the effects of a stronger Swedish crown that has appreciated by 20 percent since April 1995.
Without these two factors, another 1.5 percent could be added to the headline rate of inflation at the moment, she said.
"In contrast to the headline rate, in underlying terms the improvement on the inflation front was probably very limited," Hoyland told Reuters.

"We've expected to see the bottom in inflation for a while but the point when this will happen is being pushed further and further out so it should make the Riksbank comfortable and nudge rates a little lower in the next few months."
JP Morgan forecast the Riskbank's key interest rate, the repo, which is the central rate in a three tier system, will bottom out at between 4-4.25 percent.
Currently the repo rate stands at 4.60 percent. It started the year at 8.91 percent.

The Riksbank three weeks ago abandoned its policy of lowering the repo rate every other week and set a fixed rate for four weekly reverse repurchase operations which is more in line with the Bundesbank's practice.
The last of these fixed operations will be on November 20.
The Riksbank's two other key interest rates, the deposit and lending rates, are currently at 4.25 percent and 5.75 percent respectively.

Economist Keld Holm from Lehman Brothers forecast the repo rate would be lowered by at least another 10 basis points over the next two to four weeks on the latest figures with a trough of around 4.40 percent.
He did not expect to see any cut in the deposit and lending rates, the borders of the Riksbank's interest rate corridor.
Holm said there was no doubt the Swedish economy was a little stronger than people had expected.
"A substantial increase in disposal income - through wages increases and lower interest rates - has been partly offset by a tightening in fiscal policy," he said.
"But this substantial cut in interest rates will have quite a significant impact on people's income and we see consumption growing 1.8 percent this year and 2.7 percent in 1997."
